Welcome to the GEMINI Breeding project.

GEMINI is a platform for automated field crop phenotyping, enabling researchers to collect, process, and analyze massive amounts of high-throughput field imagery.

docs.title: GEMINI-App — Data Schema Reference
docs.text: This document describes every persistent data store: the SQLite database tables and the filesystem layout (Raw/, Intermediate/, Processed/).

docs.title: Design Philosophy & Architectural Patterns
docs.text:
GEMINI-App follows a "Local-First, High-Performance" philosophy designed for field researchers. Key patterns include:

  • Single-User Desktop Model: The application assumes a single superuser per local installation. Authentication is simplified to bypass complex JWT/OAuth flows, focusing instead on local SQLite security and filesystem permissions.
  • Extreme Denormalization for Analytics: The PlotRecord table is intentionally denormalized. It duplicates metadata from PipelineRun, Pipeline, and Workspace (e.g., experiment name, location, date). This allows the "Analyze" tab to perform lightning-fast cross-experiment queries and filtering using standard SQL without expensive joins across thousands of plot records.
  • Filesystem as the Primary Store: The SQLite database acts as a "Searchable Index" for the filesystem. Large binary data (TIFs, PNGs, point clouds) never enters the database. Instead, RunPaths handles deterministic path resolution, and the database stores relative paths to maintain portability across different data_root locations.
  • Immutability and Versioning: Processing steps (like stitching or trait extraction) do not overwrite previous results. They create new versioned directories (e.g., AgRowStitch_v2/). The database tracks the "latest" version but preserves the history of previous runs for provenance.

docs.title: Data Integrity & Validation
docs.text:
• Soft vs. Hard Deletes: The application primarily uses CASCADE deletes for parent-child relationships (e.g., deleting a Workspace deletes its Pipelines). However, filesystem data is never automatically deleted by the database engine to prevent accidental data loss of large raw datasets.
  • JSON Schema Validation: Many columns (config, steps_completed, outputs) use SQLite's JSON1 extension. While SQLModel provides Python-side validation via Pydantic, the database stores these as strings. Developers should use the SA_JSON type to ensure correct serialization.
  • Unique Constraints: Critical unique constraints are enforced on User.email and the composite (trait_record_id, plot_id) in PlotRecord to prevent duplicate trait data for the same plot in a single extraction run.

docs.title: Common Query Patterns
docs.text:
• The "Analyze" Join: To get a unified view of plots, the frontend typically queries PlotRecord filtered by workspace_id. Because PlotRecord is denormalized, no join with PipelineRun is needed for basic metadata (date, experiment, sensor), which significantly speeds up the Map and Table views.
  • Reference Matching: Matching hand-measured data to pipeline results happens via a "Identity Tuple" match: (experiment, location, population, plot_id). This is performed in Python during the GET /master-table request rather than a complex SQL join, allowing for fuzzy matching or alternate plot naming conventions if needed in the future.

docs.text:
Location (defaults):

Platform Path Linux ~/.local/share/gemi/gemi.db macOS ~/Library/Application Support/GEMI/gemi.db Windows %APPDATA%\GEMI\gemi.db

Override with SQLITE_DB_PATH=/path/to/gemi.db in .env.

docs.title: How to Add a New Database Model
docs.text:
1. Create the model file in backend/app/models/:
# backend/app/models/my_thing.py
from sqlmodel import Field, SQLModel
import uuid

class MyThing(SQLModel, table=True):
    id: uuid.UUID = Field(default_factory=uuid.uuid4, primary_key=True)
    name: str
    workspace_id: uuid.UUID = Field(foreign_key="workspace.id")
  1. Register it in backend/app/models/__init__.py so create_all sees it:
from .my_thing import MyThing  # noqa: F401

  1. Add CRUD helpers in backend/app/crud/my_thing.py.

  2. Restart the backend — the table is created automatically.

  3. Add API routes in backend/app/api/routes/, register in backend/app/api/main.py, add to hiddenimports in gemi-backend.spec.

  4. Regenerate the frontend client: bash ./scripts/generate-client.sh

  5. Update this document — add the table to SQLite Database above.

docs.title: How to Add a New File Path
docs.text:
1. Add a property or method to RunPaths in backend/app/core/paths.py:
@property
def my_new_file(self) -> Path:
    """Description — what this file contains and which step produces it."""
    return self.processed_run / "my_new_file.csv"

Use a method (not a property) when the path is versioned:

def my_versioned_dir(self, version: int) -> Path:
    return self.processed_run / f"my_dir_v{version}"
  1. Use the path in your processing function:
paths.my_new_file.write_text(content)
return {"my_new_file": paths.rel(paths.my_new_file)}
  1. Update the directory layout diagram in this document (the ASCII tree above) and the property reference table.

docs.title: App Guide
docs.text:
GEMI takes field data from upload to traits. Drone flights and rover runs become orthomosaics, per-plot images and per-plot traits. You can then chart and map those traits, and test them against marker data.

The work happens in four places, each in the sidebar:

  1. Files: upload drone images, rover logs, orthomosaics, field designs and trait tables.
  2. Process: each upload becomes a run. A run's steps turn it into plot boundaries, plot images and traits.
  3. Analyze: tables, charts and maps of the traits, plot by plot through the season.
  4. Home: a dashboard built from your data, and an agent that can do any of the above when you ask in plain words.

Genotyping holds marker data and genome-wide association studies (GWAS). Settings and Console cover setup and logs.

  1. Sections: the parts of the app.
  2. Where your data is: this computer, or a cluster session (yours, or one your group shares). Everything you see, and every job you start, lives there. Each place keeps its own experiments: switching moves nothing.
  3. Your account: sign out, and switch between light and dark themes (Appearance).
  4. Help and tours: what the page does, and a guided tour of it.

docs.title: Help on every page
docs.text:
Open Help (the ? at the top right) on any page. It explains that page and offers a step-by-step tour that points at each control. Tour of the whole app walks through every section once.

Jobs, uploads and copies in progress appear in a panel at the bottom right of every page. This includes work the agent started. Expand the panel to follow a job or cancel it.

docs.title: Aerial Pipeline
docs.text:
The aerial pipeline turns one drone flight into a field map, then into plots, plot images and per-plot traits. Each flight date is a run. Open one from the workspace's run list (see Workspaces & Runs). The steps, in order:

Step What it does Needed? 1. Data sync Checks the images are in place and reads each one's GPS position Yes (automatic) 2. Image exclusion Leave out take-off, landing, blurry or off-field images Optional 3. GCP selection Mark ground control points for accurate positions Optional, recommended 4. Orthomosaic Stitch the images into one map of the field, with an elevation model Yes 5. Plot boundaries Place the plot grid on the map and attach the field design Yes 6. Plot images One image per plot, cut from the map or picked from the raw frames For inference and viewing 7. Trait extraction Vegetation fraction, canopy height, canopy temperature per plot Yes 8. Inference Run a model on the plot images (counts, detections) Optional

A run that starts from an uploaded orthomosaic skips steps 1–4.

docs.title: 1. Data sync
docs.text: Confirms the run's images are present and reads each image's GPS position. Nothing needs doing unless the images carry no position, or a poor one (a phone camera, for example). In that case, upload the drone's flight log or a GPS track (GPS Logs: ArduPilot .bin/.log, GPX, NMEA, CSV, .pos) or a GPS table (Synced Metadata) for the same date. Start Sync lists the logs it found; positions are interpolated at each image's capture time. If the camera's clock has no time zone, it is shifted by the whole hours that fit the log, or set the zone in the dialog. The result names the logs used, the clock shift, and any images left without a position.

docs.title: 2. Image exclusion (optional)
docs.text:
Every image is a dot on a satellite map. Leave out the ones ODM should not use: take-off and landing frames, turns, blurry shots, frames off the field.

  1. Shift-drag a box over dots to leave those images out (shift-click for a single image).
  2. The count of images kept and left out.
  3. Save & complete, or Skip the step.

docs.title: 3. GCP selection (optional, recommended)
docs.text:
Ground control points (GCPs) are markers on the ground at surveyed positions. Marking them in the images ties the orthomosaic to its true position, so maps of different dates line up. ODM needs at least three GCPs marked to use them.

  1. Load GCPs from CSV: each GCP's name, latitude, longitude and elevation.
  2. The GCP you are marking. Pick one from the list.
  3. Images near it: within a radius of the GCP, or picked on the map with a lasso (Map-picker).
  4. The image map. The dots near the active GCP are highlighted, and the GCPs are drawn at their positions.

  1. Step through the images near the GCP.
  2. Click the marker's centre in the image. Right-click a mark to remove it. Mark each GCP in every photo that shows it.
  3. Save & complete writes the GCP file ODM reads. ODM uses the GCPs when at least three are marked, each in three or more photos.

docs.title: 4. Orthomosaic
docs.text:
Runs OpenDroneMap on the images (and GCPs, if marked). The result is an orthomosaic and an elevation model; the elevation model gives plant height.

Each build is kept as a version:

  • View, rename or delete a version.
  • Import existing brings in an orthomosaic made elsewhere.
  • Re-run builds again and keeps the earlier version.

Pick a quality when building:

Quality Use it for Quick (boundaries + raw frames) Placing plot boundaries and picking raw frames per plot. A 5 cm/px map from the sparse reconstruction, so wind-blown plants do not smear it. Fast. Use it when the full orthomosaic falls apart in wind. Draft Fast previews (5 cm/px). Standard Most surveys (3 cm/px). High Quality Final maps (2 cm/px). Ultra The finest maps (1 cm/px). Very slow and memory-hungry. Detailed map A 1 cm/px map for plant counts and plot images, with light 3D. Fits where Ultra runs out of memory. Custom Your own OpenDroneMap options.

The viewer (the eye icon) shows the map. It downloads as a GeoTIFF, or as a Cloud-Optimized GeoTIFF (COG) for GIS software.

docs.title: 5. Plot boundaries
docs.text:
Place one polygon per plot over the orthomosaic and attach the field design: plot number, row, column and accession. Boundaries saved for one date can be imported to another and shifted to fit.

  1. Map tools. Select an area, Add a plot, show or hide the plots, the plots' opacity, and turning the view so rows run straight (Align with plots, North up).
  2. The map. Drag a plot to move it. Shift-drag to select many, then move them together. The tools on the map's left edge draw, edit, move and delete shapes.
  3. Versions. Save the layout as a version and make it the active one (Save & complete step), or save without activating it. Load an earlier version from the list.
  4. Import from… another date's boundaries.

Below the map, Grid builds the plots for you:

  • Field design CSV: one plot per row of the design, laid out by its rows and columns. Use Flip rows, Flip cols and Swap axes if the grid comes out mirrored or turned.
  • Manual: a number of rows and columns.
  • Plot width, plot length, gaps and border rows set the plot size and spacing; 0 fits the plots to the outer boundary.
  • Boundary from ortho extent draws an outer boundary to start from. Generate plot grid fills it.
  • Import GeoJSON or Download GeoJSON to move boundaries in or out of GIS software.

Several treatments in one field

When a field was flown in parts (for example a well-watered and a drought block), the tool shows each part's orthomosaic where it is nearest. One set of boundaries can cover both, and each plot's results are kept with its treatment.

docs.title: 6. Plot images
docs.text:
One image per plot, for the plot viewer and for inference. Trait extraction does not need them. There are two sources:

  • Orthomosaic: each plot is cut out of the map.
  • Raw frames: for each plot, the flight frames that show it best (the whole plot in frame, then the most top-down). They are placed with the camera positions of the orthomosaic the boundaries were drawn on. Raw frames are sharper than the map and do not smear in wind, so a Quick orthomosaic is enough. The flight's other cameras are matched by capture time and cut the same way, so a thermal camera gives each plot a thermal image and a canopy temperature.

  1. Orthomosaic or raw frames.
  2. Which plots: all, only those without images yet, or a list (for example 12, 15-18, 106, such as a plot just added to the boundaries).
  3. Run (Pick the frames again re-picks them).
  4. What was picked: how many plots and frames, any plot only partly in frame, and how the thermal frames were matched.
  5. Camera: RGB, or the flight's other cameras.
  6. Straightened: the best frame turned top-down to the plot. Best frame: the whole frame it came from.
  7. Download the images (zip), or the manifest (CSV) of which frame each plot came from.

The thermal images are coloured on one scale for every plot. The .tif files in the download hold the temperatures.

docs.title: 7. Trait extraction
docs.text:
Measures each plot from the orthomosaic and plot boundaries:

  • Vegetation fraction: the share of the plot covered by plants.
  • Canopy height: from the elevation model.
  • Canopy temperature: from the thermal camera, when it was flown.

The results are stored per plot and appear in Analyze.

  1. Each trait's summary: its mean and range across the plots. Open it through the season (a chart) or as a table.
  2. Canopy − air temperature compares each plot's canopy temperature with the air temperature from a weather station at the flight's time. Below zero, the canopy is cooler than the air (transpiring). Upload a station's records with Add a station, pick the station and time window, then Save as a trait.

docs.title: 8. Inference
docs.text: Runs a detection, segmentation or classification model over the plot images, for example to count panicles, flowers or pods. Its counts are stored per plot as traits. See Inference & Training.

docs.title: Analyze
docs.text: Analyze shows the measured traits plot by plot through the season. Every trait lands here: from trait extraction, from models, from thermal images, from weather stations, and from reference data you uploaded. Pick an experiment, season, site and population at the top; every tab works on that choice.

docs.title: Table
docs.text:
Every plot's traits on each date, a row per plot per date.

  1. Tabs: Table, Query, Single trait, Multivariate, Map, Weather.
  2. Experiment, season, site and population (crop).
  3. Traits shown. Also traits not measured here adds traits from other experiments and sites.
  4. Each date, or one date.
  5. Filter plots by plot number (plot:12), accession (acc:CB27), date (date:2022-07) or any text.
  6. Download CSV.

Click a row to see that plot's image on that date.

docs.title: Query
docs.text:
Find plots and see their images across the season, with each date's traits under the image.

  1. Find plots by plot number or accession. An accession adds all of its plots.
  2. The plots you added. Remove one with its ×, or clear them all.
  3. Image source and size. Plot images from the orthomosaic, the raw frames or the thermal camera; small, medium or large. Only dates with images hides the empty dates.
  4. Each plot through the season, a row per plot and a column per date. Click an image to open it full size.

docs.title: Single trait
docs.text:
Pick a trait to see it through the season, plot by plot, or across genotypes and sites.

Chart type:

  • Through the season: the mean, the middle half of the plots, and the range on each date.
  • Season table: a plot per row, a date per column.
  • Histogram.

Outliers are left out by default; Include outliers shows them. Narrow the chart by experiment, season, site, dataset or population.

docs.title: Multivariate
docs.text:
Several traits together:

  • Correlation: which traits rise and fall together.
  • PCA: the main axes of variation across plots.
  • MANOVA: whether genotypes differ across several traits at once.

Average replicates by genotype correlates genotype means instead of single plots. Pick the experiments, seasons, sites and traits, then Run analysis.

docs.title: Map
docs.text:
Each date's orthomosaic with its plots coloured by a trait.

  1. Date.
  2. Colour plots by a trait (a heatmap), or show outlines only.
  3. The orthomosaic under the plots, with the opacity of each layer.

Click a plot for its traits and image.

docs.title: Weather
docs.text: Weather station records beside the flights: the air temperature through each flight day, with the flight's window shaded. A table compares each flight's canopy temperature with the air temperature (CTD, canopy − air), along with humidity, vapour pressure deficit (VPD) and light (PAR). Each treatment can have its own station. Upload station records as Weather Data in Files, or with Add a station.

docs.title: Home: Dashboard & Agent
docs.text: Home has two tabs: the Dashboard, an overview built from your trait data, and the Agent, an assistant that does the work for you. You can turn either off in Settings → Application → Home.

docs.title: Dashboard
docs.text:
1. Dashboard or agent.
  2. Experiment and crop: the dashboard covers one experiment, site and season, and one crop.
  3. What needs you in Process: runs that stopped with an error or need your input. Open Process goes there.
  4. Pin a card to keep it on your own tab, or Hide it.
  5. Your own tabs (My views). + adds one.

The overview's cards:

  • The data: plots, dates, traits and sites.
  • Traits over the season: each trait's plot mean on each date, with a one-line summary of what changed.
  • Which traits move together: correlations between traits.
  • Which traits are heritable: broad-sense heritability (H²) of each trait, from a mixed model.
  • BLUPs: each accession's estimated genetic value per trait, to rank lines.

docs.title: Agent
docs.text:
The agent does in the app what you ask in plain words. It can:

  • upload data;
  • run pipeline steps and mark plots;
  • check jobs and tell you why one failed;
  • answer questions about the traits;
  • run a GWAS.

It follows skills: written procedures for each kind of task. Its runs, and anything it changed, carry a small robot mark in Process.

  1. Past runs of the agent; New run starts another.
  2. Skills: the procedures it can follow, each with the kind of request it is for.
  3. Pick a skill, or let the agent decide.
  4. What to work on, in words: for example the Davis rover run of 2026-09-17. The agent finds the run.
  5. The task: what the agent should do.
  6. The model the agent thinks with, and the compute it uses.

Some example requests:

  • "Process the drone flight of 2026-08-17 at Davis up to the plot images."
  • "Which jobs failed this week, and why?"
  • "Is panicle count related to canopy height in the sorghum?"
  • "Run a GWAS of flowering time at Riverside 2015."

The agent works through the same app, so everything it does shows in Process, Analyze and the jobs panel like your own work.

docs.title: Genotyping
docs.text: Genotyping holds marker data for your lines and genome-wide association studies (GWAS) of measured traits against those markers.

docs.title: Studies
docs.text:
A study is one marker set, such as a SNP panel, linked to the experiments whose lines it genotypes. Each card shows:

  • the study's size (markers × samples);
  • its experiments;
  • how many GWAS runs it has, and the latest result;
  • thumbnails of its Manhattan plots.

New study brings in a marker file: HapMap, VCF, PLINK or CSV. The sample names must match the experiment's line or accession names.

docs.title: A study
docs.text: Overview shows the study's GWAS runs as tiles, newest first. Each tile gives the trait, the environment (site and season), how many markers pass the Bonferroni threshold, how many lines were tested, and the genomic inflation λ. Open a tile for its plots and strongest markers.

docs.title: Run a GWAS
docs.text:
New GWAS sets up a run:

  • Source data: the experiment, the trait dataset and the traits to test.
  • Environment: a site and a season. Each line's values are averaged over every site and season you include; one environment gives a cleaner test.
  • Model: a linear mixed model with a kinship matrix, plus principal components as covariates.
  • QC thresholds: minor allele frequency, missingness, and how replicates are combined.

docs.title: A GWAS run
docs.text:
The run page shows:

  • a summary: model, test, markers and samples before and after QC, principal components used, genomic inflation λ, and markers passing the Bonferroni, genome-wide and suggestive thresholds;
  • the Manhattan and QQ plots;
  • the strongest markers.

Download sumstats saves the full results table.

docs.title: Import TASSEL results
docs.text: GWAS runs done in TASSEL (GLM or MLM) can sit beside the app's own. Import TASSEL results takes TASSEL's statistics table (for an MLM export, the file ending in _2.txt). It draws the same Manhattan and QQ plots.

docs.title: Ground Pipeline
docs.text:
The ground pipeline processes images taken along the rows: a rover such as a Farm-ng Amiga driving the beds, or a person carrying a phone or camera (handheld). Each plot's stretch of frames is marked. Its plot images are then either stitched into one image of the plot, or taken from the plot's own raw frames. Those images go to Analyze and can be run through a model.

Rover: upload the .bin logs as Farm-ng Binary File. Handheld: upload the photos as Image Data with platform Handheld (see Upload). Create a Ground pipeline in the workspace, then add a run for the upload.

Step What it does 1. Data sync Gives every frame its position: the rover log's GPS, or the photos' own GPS or a GPS log 2. Plot marking Marks the start and end frame of every plot 3. Stitching (optional) Stitches each plot's frames into one image (AgRowStitch) and georeferences it 4. Plot boundaries One polygon per plot with the field design attached (for the stitched plots) 5. Plot images Each plot's images: its stitched image, its raw frames, or one photo per plot 6. Inference Runs a model on the plot images (optional)

Which way through depends on the images:

Images Positions Plot images from Rover its log's GPS stitched plots, or raw frames Handheld, with GPS the photos' own GPS (phone location on), or a GPS log carried on the walk stitched plots, or raw frames, like a rover Handheld walk, no GPS none raw frames, paired with the field design in marking order Handheld, one photo per plot, no GPS none each photo paired with a plot of the field design

docs.title: 1. Data sync
docs.text:
Rover: the frames and GPS track are extracted from the log; nothing needs doing.

Handheld: each photo gets its position and capture time. Start Sync shows where they come from:

  • The photos' own GPS, as the camera wrote it. A phone does this when location is on for its camera.
  • A GPS log of the walk, uploaded as GPS Logs for the same date and camera: a GPX or CSV from a GPS app, an NMEA file, or an RTK receiver's .pos or CSV. The position at each photo's capture time is interpolated between the log's fixes, so it beats a phone's own GPS. The dialog lists the logs it found.
  • Camera clock: photos are matched to the log by time. Phones record their time zone; many cameras keep local time without it, and are shifted by the whole hours that line them up with the log. Set the zone yourself if you know it.

The result says how many photos got a position and from where, which logs were used, and any clock shift. Photos with no GPS at all are fine: the step says so, and their plots are paired with the field design in the Plot images step.

iPhone photos

Upload JPEGs. Apple's HEIC format can't be processed: set Settings → Camera → Formats → Most Compatible, or export the photos as JPEG with their location.

docs.title: 2. Plot marking
docs.text:
Each plot is a stretch of frames between a start frame and an end frame. Open the tool with Open Tool on the step.

  1. Keys: arrow keys move through the frames, S marks the start, E the end, N starts a new plot, D deletes one, Ctrl+S saves. Plots per frame (beside them) is for passes that see more than one plot at once, one per band of the frame.
  2. The frame you are on. Zoom with the wheel or the buttons; the Step setting skips several frames at a time.
  3. Mark start / end of the current plot.
  4. Plot by plot: go to a plot by number, or step through them. + adds a plot, the bin deletes it.
  5. Every plot on the track as a strip: green is marked, amber needs a check (a marking carried over from another date, or a frame that no longer exists). Click a segment to go to that plot.
  6. Check a plot: its start and end frames are shown side by side. Looks right · next (Y) confirms it and moves on. Set the stitching direction for the plot below it.
  7. GPS map: the track, with the current frame on it.
  8. Mark automatically marks the whole track from the crop rows. It uses the plots per bed and the plot spacing recorded for the run; review the result afterwards.
  9. Save, or Save As a new version. Saved versions are listed above the buttons.

When the field was also flown with a drone, Mark from drone plot boundaries marks every plot from the boundaries drawn on that date's orthomosaic, and the plots keep their drone plot names.

docs.title: 3. Stitching (optional)
docs.text:
AgRowStitch stitches each marked plot's frames into one panoramic image of the plot. It then georeferences the plots and makes a combined mosaic. Stitching needs the frames' positions; for images with no GPS, use the raw frames instead.

  1. Stitch version. Each stitch is kept as a version; pick one to see it.
  2. Download the combined mosaic, or every plot's image (zip).
  3. The stitched plots, a page at a time.

Stitching settings (cropping, direction and others) are in the pipeline's Settings. If some plots fail or look wrong, change the settings and run the step again. Re-run asks before it starts.

docs.title: 4. Plot boundaries
docs.text: The same tool as in the aerial pipeline (see Plot boundaries), drawn over the stitched mosaic. Boundaries can also be generated from the stitched plots themselves. The raw frames use boundaries only to name plots by GPS; plots marked from drone boundaries, or paired with a field design, need none.

docs.title: 5. Plot images
docs.text:
Choose where each plot's images come from:

  • Stitched plots: each stitched plot is matched to the boundary that contains it, by GPS. Show matches lists them; Show plot images shows the images.
  • Raw frames: each marked plot's own frames, from its start to its end, without stitching. Consecutive frames are aligned with each other, and only frames that don't overlap are kept for counting (the plot's tiles); its middle frame is its plot image. A model's counts on the tiles add up to the plot's count without counting a plant twice. Plots are named from the drone boundaries they were marked from, else by their GPS inside the plot boundaries. With no GPS, add the field design: its rows are paired with the plots in the order they were marked, so list the plots in the order walked.
  • One photo per plot: for handheld photos with no GPS, taken one at each plot. Choose the field design; each photo is paired with a plot, by a column of the design naming the photo (image, photo, file…), else in file-name order. The pairing is shown in full before anything is made; nothing in the photos can confirm it afterwards.

The plot images appear in Analyze → Query and in the plot viewer beside the drone's.

docs.title: 6. Inference
docs.text:
Runs a model on the plot images, for example to count flowers. For raw frames, pick the image source Every frame of each plot, no overlap (counts summed): each plot's count is the sum over its tiles. See Inference & Training.

Let the agent do it

The agent's ground-pipeline skill covers rover and handheld runs: syncing positions from a GPS log, marking plots, and plot images from the stitch or the raw frames. Ask it on the Home page, for example: "mark the plots on the Coachella rover run of 2026-09-17 and make plot images from the raw frames".

docs.title: Inference & Training
docs.text:
Inference runs a trained model over a run's plot images. Models can detect and count things (panicles, flowers, pods, seedlings), segment them, or classify plots. A model's per-plot counts are stored as traits and appear in Analyze like any other trait. The step is the last one of both pipelines. Open it with Open Tool (or Re-open Tool) on a run's Inference step.

Models can come from:

  • Roboflow: a model ID and an API key.
  • Hugging Face: including zero-shot detectors that find objects from a text description.
  • Your own weights: a model trained here, or uploaded.

Keys for Roboflow and Hugging Face are saved under Settings → Keys & tokens.

docs.title: Results on a run
docs.text:
1. Run a model on this date's plot images.
  2. Label & train: label images and train a model of your own (see below).
  3. Each model's runs on this date, newest first: how many plots and the mean count per plot. View results opens the detections.

docs.title: Run a model
docs.text:
1. Model: one set up for the pipeline (Set up models), or any saved one.
  2. Image source: plot images from the orthomosaic, straightened views from the raw frames, whole raw images, or, for ground runs whose plot images came from the raw frames, every frame of each plot, no overlap (counts summed): each plot's count is the sum over its non-overlapping frames, so no plant is counted twice.
  3. Run on the image shown (to try the model) or on every image of the date.
  4. Preview: step through the plot images.

To run a model on every date at once, use Run across dates on the workspace's run list (see Workspaces & Runs).

docs.title: Check the results
docs.text:
1. Confidence: hide detections below a threshold, and see the counts change.
  2. Use this threshold in Analyze: the per-plot counts in Analyze use it from then on. Tick other dates to apply it to the same model on the other dates.
  3. Label: correct the boxes on this image (see below).
  4. Plots, sorted by plot number or by count. Very high or very low counts are the first to check.
  5. The detections on the plot. Zoom with the wheel and drag to move. Arrow keys step through the plots.

CSV downloads the counts.

docs.title: Label & train
docs.text:
When no model counts what you need, or counts it badly in your conditions, label some images and train one. Glare, a different growth stage or another camera are common reasons.

  • Start from a model's detections: the model's boxes are a first draft. Correct them, adding what it missed and removing what it got wrong.
  • Start blank: draw the boxes by hand, or find objects from an example box or a description.

Labelled images are kept as a set, one set per kind of object, shared across dates. Train fits a model on the set. Include labelled images from several dates, so the model sees different light and growth stages. When training finishes, the new model appears in the model list for every run.

Compare plots within a date

Counts from images depend on the light: sunny dates often count fewer flowers than overcast ones. Compare plots within one date, and look at trends across dates with that in mind.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text:
Application

  • Home: show the dashboard, the agent, or both.
  • Data & services: where the data is stored and which services the app talks to.
  • Compute: see below.
  • Sign-in.
  • About.

docs.title: Compute
docs.text:
Where the processing runs: this computer, or a cluster. Each kind of job has its own worker:

  • rover extraction;
  • stitching;
  • orthomosaic;
  • map tiles and plot images;
  • models and traits;
  • genome-wide association;
  • the agent's language model.

A worker starts when a job needs it and stops after a while with no jobs. For each worker you can see whether it is running, start or stop it, and choose where it runs (Run on).

On a cluster, Share this session with my group lets members of your group join the same session: they start their own workers on their own allocation and work on the same data.

docs.title: Keys & tokens
docs.text:
• A Hugging Face access token, for gated or private models.
  • A Roboflow API key, for Roboflow models.

Keys are saved with your account and used by any model that has no key of its own. Only you can see them.

Account changes your name and password. People sets who each experiment belongs to: a public experiment shows in everyone's lists, a private one only in the lists of the people linked to it. Administrators can add people there.

docs.title: Console
docs.text: The running log of the app, the agent and the jobs, for when something seems stuck. Filter it by source (the jobs on the cluster, the agent, the app) or by text, and copy it to share.

docs.title: Upload
docs.text: Everything starts in Files → Upload. You choose what kind of data it is and describe where it belongs (experiment, season, site, crop, date, platform, camera). Then you point the app at the files. The description decides where the data is stored. It also becomes the filter you use later in Process and Analyze, so keep names consistent across uploads.

docs.title: 1. Pick the kind of data
docs.text:
1. Pick the kind of data. Choose one of:

    • Image Data: drone or handheld photos (JPEG, PNG or TIFF; iPhone HEIC photos are refused, with how to get JPEGs).
    • Farm-ng Binary File: Amiga rover logs.
    • Orthomosaic: a map made elsewhere.
    • Field Design: plot, row, column and accession of every plot.
    • Reference Data: hand measurements per plot.
    • Weather Data: weather station records.
    • Trait Data: traits measured elsewhere.
    • Genomic Data: marker files.
    • GPS Logs and Synced Metadata: a drone's flight log, or the GPS track of a walk or drive (GPX, NMEA, CSV from a phone logger or RTK receiver, RTKLIB/Emlid .pos), or a GPS table, for images whose own positions are missing or poor.

    Each type shows a short hint in the list of what it is for. 2. Or continue a recent upload. Another date of a field you have uploaded before fills in everything except the date.

docs.title: 2. Describe the data
docs.text:
1. Data type: what you picked above.
  2. Experiment, season, site and population (crop). Pick existing ones or type new names. A flight over several neighbouring trials can use Mixed: the field design's crop column then files each plot's results under its own crop.
  3. Date. Enter one date, or let the app read it from the file names. Either way you confirm it before anything is uploaded.
  4. Platform and camera. Drone, rover or handheld (handheld photos with GPS go through the ground pipeline like a rover's; without GPS they are paired with the field design, see Ground pipeline); RGB, thermal, the drone's own camera, or another camera by name. Each camera is stored in its own folder, so an RGB and a thermal camera flown on the same date never mix.
  5. Where the files are. See the next section.
  6. The upload area. Drop files or whole folders here, or click to browse. Subfolders are included.

Further down the form:

  • Treatment (optional). Use this when an experiment's data is collected separately per treatment, for example a well-watered and a drought block flown as two flights. Each treatment is kept as its own upload. Its runs are processed together, but the results stay apart.
  • Diurnal data. Tick this when the field was covered more than once on the same date. Each pass then becomes its own run.

docs.title: 3. Where the files are
docs.text:
This computer: drop or browse files as above.

On the cluster: when the app runs on a cluster, type the folder's full path there. Look lists what is in it before anything is copied. The files are uploaded by a job on the cluster and never pass through your computer.

Online storage: Box, Google Drive, Dropbox, S3, WebDAV, a web folder or SFTP. Connect an account once and browse its folders. A job copies the folder straight from the storage, so nothing passes through your computer. To take only some files, give the ending their names share (for example _V.JPG).

docs.title: 4. Check what is stored
docs.text:
Uploads run in the background and appear in the jobs panel at the bottom right.

Manage lists each experiment's uploads and results by season. Deleting an experiment removes everything it holds. Reference data tables are listed below the experiments. They appear as extra columns in Analyze → Table for the matching experiment and site.

View counts what the app holds (experiments, datasets, traits, sensors, populations, genotyping studies). It also shows trait records and uploaded images, filtered to an experiment.

Uploading by asking

The agent on the Home page can upload too. For example: "upload the drone flight in /data/2026-08-17/RGB to GEMINI-26, Davis, Sorghum".

docs.title: Workspaces & Runs
docs.text:
Process is where uploads are turned into results:

  • A workspace groups the pipelines of one field experiment.
  • A pipeline holds the processing settings for one kind of data: Aerial for drone images, Ground for Amiga rover runs.
  • Each upload processed by a pipeline is a run: one date, one flight or rover pass.

docs.title: Workspaces
docs.text:
1. New workspace: give it a name and a short description.
  2. By workspace or by experiment. By experiment lists every run by experiment and date, whatever workspace it is in.
  3. A workspace card shows previews of its latest runs, how many runs are in each pipeline, and how many need you (input needed, failed, complete). Runs started or changed by the agent carry a small robot mark.

docs.title: A workspace's runs
docs.text:
Open a workspace to see its runs: one row per date, one column per step.

  1. New run: pick an uploaded dataset to process.
  2. Run across dates: run the same steps on every date at once (see below).
  3. Filter runs by status or crop.
  4. One column per step. The header counts how many dates have that step done.
  5. Click any cell to open that date at that step. A tick means done. next is what that date needs next.
  6. Several runs on one date (a field flown in parts, several treatments, or diurnal passes) fold into one row. Expand it for a row per run.
  7. Add another pipeline, for example a ground pipeline beside the aerial one.

Settings holds the pipeline's processing settings: orthomosaic quality, stitching parameters and models.

docs.title: Run across dates
docs.text:
Starts the same steps on every date of the pipeline and skips dates where a step is already done. Tick the steps to run:

  • Quick orthomosaic: a fast map per flight, enough to place plot boundaries and pick raw frames.
  • Plot images: from the orthomosaic, or from the raw frames.
  • Trait extraction.
  • Inference, with one or more models per crop.

Under Image source, set the order in which each date's plot images are tried. The table at the bottom shows each date's progress.

docs.title: A run
docs.text:
A run page shows one step at a time.

  1. What this run is on: experiment, site, crop, date, platform, camera, the treatments flown, and how many images were found.
  2. Cameras of this flight. A flight can carry more than one camera, for example a thermal camera beside the RGB one. Every camera's upload belongs to the one run:
    • The RGB camera builds the orthomosaic, the boundaries and the traits.
    • The other cameras' frames are matched to the RGB frames by capture time. They go into the plot images, and a thermal camera also gives each plot's canopy temperature. Nothing needs doing for that.
    • When the field was flown in parts (for example one flight per treatment), each camera's row lists those parts. An orthomosaic of another camera is optional, and can be built per part from here.
  3. Pick a step. Each step shows its status in the list.
  4. The step bar: one segment per step, coloured by status (done, to do, running, failed, skipped). Click a segment to open that step.
  5. Next / previous step. A step unlocks once what it needs is done. Hover a locked arrow to see what is left.

Go to the step to do next jumps to the first step still to do. Any finished step can be re-run; the earlier result is kept as a version.

The steps of each pipeline are described in Aerial Pipeline and Ground Pipeline.

docs.title: Hardware Overview
docs.text: Placeholder for Hardware documentation.

docs.title: Getting Started with the farm-ng Amiga
docs.text:
1. Control the Amiga.
    • Go through the dashboard overview. We recommend getting comfortable with the speed adjustment and e-stop configuration.
    • We recommend going 100 - 200 ft/min (the first 2 major ticks) to get the best image quality. See the farm-ng Amiga Dashboard Documentation for more information on use of the dashboard.
  2. Set up the GPS RTK base station.
    • Connect the powerbrick to the CAN/POWER input on the back of the Brain. It will start doing its serve and pinning its position.
    • The base station will get some time to have a good accuracy. Marcelo recommends you power it up, use the UI to connect to WIFI, and leave static for at least 20 min before connecting to receive corrections.
    • Once the base station is connected, you should see the GPS icon at the top right of the Brain without the slash.

  3. Record some sample images in a field or with random objects.

    • Follow the farm-ng Camera App Documentation on how to start and stop a recording.
    • Have the GPS and the top camera (facing down) centered on the Amiga.
    • The side cameras can be placed as low as possible. Play around with the angle of the side cameras and preview the images from the Brain.

  4. Export the recorded file.

    • You will need a USB drive plugged into the back of the brain. Make sure to only plug in the drive after the brain has been turned on.
    • Open the file manager app to view the images and export. Refer to the farm-ng File Manager App Documentation for more information on using the file manager for viewing and exporting.

docs.title: Data Saving and Export SOPs
docs.text:
• The GEMINI App will be used for extraction of the binary files recorded using the Amiga. Follow the app installation and setup instructions before proceeding.
  • Once you are done recording, use the file manager app to export the binary files to an external drive.
    • Note that the USB drive must be ext4 or exFAT formatted. USB 3.0 drives are recommended for faster file-transfer.
    • Once data has been successfully transferred to the drive, the files in the file manager can be deleted.
  • Using the upload tab of the GEMINI App, upload the binary files to begin extracting the binary files to viewable formats.
    • Viewing of the extracted data will be added soon to the GEMINI App.

docs.title: Select Topics
docs.text:
• Before recording, ensure that the following topics are being recorded by going into your settings and going to the Recorder tab.
  • To include the topics, press the Include URI button next to the topic name.
  • The following topics should be selected for recording (create a profile if needed):
GPS Topics Oak0 Topics Oak1 Topics Oak2 Topics /gps/ecef oak/0/calibration oak/1/calibration oak/2/calibration /gps/pvt oak/0/disparity oak/1/disparity oak/2/disparity /gps/relposned oak/0/imu oak/1/imu oak/2/imu oak/0/rgb oak/1/rgb oak/2/rgb

docs.title: Image Quality Assurance
docs.text:
• Take a sample recording while driving the Amiga to the field (at the speed you hope to drive the Amiga through the field).
  • View the recording in the file manager app to observe any issues with blur, exposure, occlusion, shadows, or camera position / perspective.
    • Use the dropdown in the top left to toggle which Oak camera's recording is shown.
  • Before beginning recording for the day, use the settings icon in the Camera App to show each camera's output on the display.
    • Use the Auto Exposure and Auto Focus buttons to recalibrate each camera if there appears to be an issue.
  • Once you have verified that the image quality looks correct, recording can begin once the GPS RTK connection has been made.

docs.title: GPS Quality Assurance
docs.text:
• Connect GPS Base Station to WiFi and ensure that the attena is connected to the base station.
  • It is recommended that the attena is placed outside with a clear view of the sky.
  • Connect the Amiga to WiFi as well and go to the settings GPS NTRIP tab.
  • NOTE: The Amiga and Base Station DO NOT need to be on the same WiFi network, but they do need to be connected to the internet.
  • Ensure that a green notification appears in the top right corner of the screen indicating that the GPS is connected to the base station.

docs.title: Data Collection
docs.text:
• Please go through the Pre-Data Collection steps before proceding.
  • We assume your field experiment is split into columns and rows.
  • Drive your Amiga to the start of the first column and press the Record button in the Camera Recorder App.
  • The Amiga will begin recording the camera data and GPS data.
  • At the end of the first column, press the Stop button in the Camera Recorder App.
  • If you have different experiments in the same column, you may stop recording at any point and start a new recording.
  • However, it is difficult to track recordings if you stop and start recording multiple times in the same column.

docs.title: Autoplot Prerequisites
docs.text: • Open the Settings tab from the Brain home screen.

docs.title: IMU Calibration
docs.text:
• If you have not calibrated the rover IMU or have made recent changes to the rover, use the IMU Calibration settings pane to calibrate.
  • With the rover on flat ground, click Start Calibration to begin.
  • You will see a popup to remind you to move the rover to flat ground. Click Confirm to continue. Calibration should complete within a few seconds.

docs.title: Robot Geometry
docs.text:
• The autoplot app requires accurate robot geometry information to be entered in the brain.
  • Measure the wheelbase and track width using a tape measure.
  • Find the center point of the amiga using these measurements.
  • Measure the placement of the top camera (OAK0) for IMU Offset and the GPS antenna for GPS Offset relative to this center point.
  • The x and y offset definitions can be seen in the image below (via farm-ng). Facing the direction of the dashboard, negative y values are defined as right of the center point while negative x values are defined as behind the center point.
  • Once the offsets have been found, update the values in the Robot Geometry pane of the settings tab.
  • Click Apply to save the robot geometry and proceed.

docs.title: GPS NTRIP / WiFi
docs.text:
• Ensure base station credentials are populated in the GPS NTRIP settings pane.
  • When GPS is properly connected, the GPS symbol will not be crossed out and the GPS RTK CONNECTED message will be present on the GPS NTRIP tab, as seen here.
  • Make sure the amiga is connected to WiFi.

docs.title: Path Creation
docs.text:
• After satisfying the prerequisites, open the Autoplot app from the amiga Brain.
  • After some load time, two camera streams will be visible on the left side of the screen.
  • To create a new path, click the New Path button. Begin driving the amiga along the path using the pendant.
  • When you've reached the end of the desired path, click Save Path and give the recorded path a name. If you deviate from the desired path, you can click Pause and Remove Point to fix the path before resuming recording.

docs.title: Path Following
docs.text:
• To follow a path, click the Load Path button to see the saved path recordings. Select the path you'd like to load.
  • Now, the dashboard has to be set to auto-control mode to start the path.
  • On the dashboard, click the A symbol to open the auto control tab.
  • In the auto control tab, press the AUTO CONTROL button to turn auto control on.
  • Once auto control has been turned on and all other prerequisites have been met, the status indicators on the amiga Brain should be as shown:
  • If there are no issues, the Start Path button can now be clicked in the Autoplot app. Path following will work best if you Start Path with the amiga close to the starting point facing the same direction as when the recording was started.

docs.title: Debugging
docs.text:
• If any prerequisite service on the status bar is crossed out, click the icon for more information.
  • If the Start Path button is still shows a question mark, press the button for information on the error.
  • Errors related to GPS accuracy can be avoided by adjusting the thresholds in the Robot Localization settings pane.
  • Guidelines on adjustment of the distance and time thresholds are provided within the settings pane. We recommend increasing the Path Deviation Threshold and Minimum GPS Accuracy values to avoid errors. The exact values to increase to should be determined by in-field testing and may vary based on distance from RTK base station.
  • To adjust the speed of the amiga in auto control mode, open the Track Following settings pane and adjust values as needed.
  • A maximum linear speed of 0.5 to 1 m/s is recommended to maximize image quality.

docs.title: Device Access
docs.text:
• The amiga brain must be connected to WiFi for any on-device app development.
  • Follow the farm-ng documentation on requesting device SSH access and configuring SSH keys.
  • Follow the Tailscale quickstart guide using the same Google account used in your farm-ng fleet manager login for your tailnet login.
  • Add the device you intend to develop from to your tailnet. Marcelo will share the link to add your amiga to your tailnet.

docs.title: VSCode
docs.text:
• VSCode is recommended for app development on the amiga.
  • With Tailscale active on your device (using sudo tailscale up on Linux or opening the app on Windows or Mac), find the amiga's IP-address.
  • Follow the instructions from farm-ng for configuration of SSH connections using VSCode.

docs.title: UI Testing
docs.text:
• To develop apps without physical access to the brain, a method to view the UI is needed.
  • After configuring and opening Tailscale, type the brain IP address into a browser.
  • After some load time, the brain UI should be visible in the browser.

docs.title: farm-ng App Templates
docs.text:
• farm-ng provides app templates that can be used to simplify app development together with app examples.
  • Depending on your preference, you can use the ReactJS farm-ng app guide or Kivy farm-ng app guide to start developing.

  • Using Github, create a new personal repository from the desired app template: Kivy Template / ReactJS Template

  • After clicking Create a new repository, name your new app repository and add a description as desired. Choose whether the repository should be public or private. Click Create repository when finished.

docs.title: Cloning the New App
docs.text:
• The new app now needs to be cloned to the amiga brain for development.
  • Open a new VSCode window. Open the source control tab from the left sidebar.
  • Click Clone repository. Next, either choose Clone from Github or paste in the repository URL from the repository's Code button.
  • If you have not previously set up Git credentials for cloning repositories, follow the Github docs on remote repositories and cloning methods.

docs.title: Running the App
docs.text:
• After cloning the repository and developing the app using the examples and information shown in the ReactJS farm-ng app guide or Kivy farm-ng app guide, the app can be tested.
  • For apps using the UI, go to the amiga IP address in a browser to see and interact with the brain.
  • In the VSCode terminal, locate the entry.sh script to be used to open the app.
  • Make the script executable by entering sudo chmod +x entry.sh in the terminal.
  • Run ./entry.sh. The app or any error starting the app should be seen on the UI. Logging information on the app start will be shown in the terminal.
  • Make sure to change the path saved in the exec_cmd field to the correct entry.sh location and the display_name to the app name in the manifest.json file to allow the app to properly launch from the UI and be displayed on the apps screen.
  • When the app is finished and the ability to launch from the UI is desired, make the install.sh script executable as shown before and run the script to add the app icon to the apps screen.

docs.title: Propeller Assembly Instructions
docs.text:
The GEMINI quadcopter is based on Arducopter, and the motor layout follows their QUAD X configuration.

Assemble the propellers by matching the motors' rotation direction with the propellers' rotation direction. The correct propeller rotation direction is the one that pushes air downwards when spinning. The correct orientation can be illustrated below when holding the propeller at eye level and looking at the blades.

Install the propellers onto the motor mounts using the included M3 screws. Tighten the screws firmly enough to prevent the propellers from detaching during flight. However, be careful not to overtighten, as this could damage the propeller and the motor threads.

docs.title: DJI Phantom 4 for GEMINI Sensing
docs.text:
A 3D-printable model has been developed to mount an iPhone under the DJI Phantom 4 for remote sensing.

Download STL files: Phantom4_iPhone13_Mount_Legs | Phantom4_iPhone13_Mount_Tray

For printing, PETG filament is recommended over PLA due to its greater heat resistance. Follow the extruder temperature and the manufacturer's recommended temperature for the filament. After 3D printing, use a heat gun to bend the drone legs to the desired angle. Bending the legs provides better stability during landing and prevents them from appearing in the field of view when simultaneously capturing video with the DJI gimbal camera.

For PETG, set the heat gun temperature to 230 degrees Celsius.

When bending the legs outward, the outer side is more prone to tearing due to greater length deformation. Therefore, apply heat evenly to the outer side to make the bending area pliable. However, avoid excessive heat, as this can cause damage.

After applying heat, place the leg on a flat surface and bend it. If the angle is insufficient, apply additional heat to the bending area with the heat gun to achieve the desired angle.

Assemble the bent leg parts and the tray part using M3 15mm pan head screws. Then, insert the wire that secures the assembly to the drone legs.

docs.title: Installing Mission Planner
docs.text:
You can follow the instructions from Installing Mission Planner — Mission Planner documentation

For Android Tablets, you can download and install this APK file:

  • Release Android Development Build · ArduPilot/MissionPlanner · GitHub

docs.title: Using a Tablet or PC?
docs.text: You can connect the drone to an android tablet using USB OTG, the same as a PC. Using a tablet, you can monitor the drone's status and telemetry data when you are out in the field. However, using a laptop PC is recommended if you want to change detailed settings.

docs.title: How to Make Survey Missions in Mission Planner
docs.text:
1. Open the Mission Planner program.
  1. Click "Plan".
  1. The home location will be used as a starting point when you're making the flight missions. If you connect the drone, you can see where the home position is. If you can't see the maps of your field, you can manually set the home location by entering the Latitude and Longitude or clicking on the map.

For example, the UC Davis RMI Vineyard location is: Latitude: 38.5323259361796 Longitude: -121.752081513405

You can also set the default altitude for your waypoints by setting "Default Alt".

  1. Draw a Polygon using the right-click menu → Polygon → Draw a Polygon.

  1. To create a survey mission, right-click → Auto WP → Survey (Grid).

  1. You can see the generated paths, but you have to modify the parameters. Click "Advanced Options". It will show more settings.

  1. Select the Camera to estimate the camera's field of view.

  • Choose FLIR Vue 336 6.8mm because the FLIR One Pro's FOV is 50x40 and FLIR Vue 336 6.8mm is 45x35.

  • Set the flight speed. Recommended speed: 2m/s ~ 4m/s.

  • Check the total flight time and the period for Photo every.

  • Optimize the Polygon by only showing the Polygons and move the points.

  • Make sure the flight time is within the drone's max flight time (20 minutes).

  • Check "Use speed for this mission", "Add Takeoff and Land WPs", and "Use RTL" if you want the drone to automatically land at the launch point after the mission.

  • Click "Accept".

  • Save the polygon and waypoints to a file.

  • Save polygon just in case it's needed again.

  • Save the waypoint file to reload the waypoints to the program

  • Write the waypoints to the drone when it's connected to the Mission Planner Software.

docs.title: How to Prepare the Drone Flight
docs.text:
1. Open the box and bring out the drone.
  1. Mount the iPhone and FLIR One Pro to the tray.
  1. Expand the arm until it's clicked to the arm clip.
  1. Install the Li-Po battery and tie it.
  1. Power up the drone and plug the USB Radio module into your computer. Be aware of the plus and minus of the connector.
  1. Open the Mission Planner Application.
  1. Select AUTO and Click Connect. It will automatically scan the port and find the USB radio module.
  1. Now you can see the location and status of the drone.
  1. Press the hardware safety switch to activate the drone.

  1. Arm the motors by pressing the left stick to the lower right corner and hold it.

    Note: GEMINI drone controller is MODE 2 to comply with most recent drone pilots. If you want to change the controller setting, please refer below:

    • What is the difference between Mode 1 and Mode 2?
    • Flysky FS-i6X Transmitter Mode 1 To Mode 2 Modification
    • FlySky FSi6 - MODE 1 or MODE 2 Setup

  2. Now you can fly the drone.

  3. To disarm the motors after the flight, press the left stick to the lower left corner and hold it.

docs.title: How to Start the Auto Mission
docs.text:
1. Follow the instructions from "How to prepare the drone flight"

  2. Write the waypoints to the drone when it's connected to the Mission Planner Software.

  1. Press the hardware safety switch to activate the drone.

  1. Arm the motors by pressing the left stick to the lower right corner and hold it.

  1. Lift the Throttle to 20~30% and Toggle the Auto switch. It will automatically launch and start the mission.

  1. If you set auto landing, it will return to the launch position and automatically land. If you did not set the auto return, it will stay at the last waypoint in the Mission, and you will have to land the drone manually.

docs.title: How to Use Drone Battery Charger
Introduction
docs.text: This document explains how to charge a drone battery using a drone battery charger. After reading this, you will know how to charge a drone battery, how to set the battery voltage to storage mode after a flight, precautions to take when charging the battery, and how to respond in case of errors.

docs.title: Battery Specs
docs.text: GEMINI Custom drones come with 7000 ~ 10000 mAh Lithium polymer batteries. The maximum possible flight time varies depending on the battery capacity and the drone's payload, but generally, about 25 minutes of flight is possible.

docs.title: Charger Specs
docs.text: For this project, we use a charger capable of balance charging lithium polymer batteries. Balance charging means equalizing the voltage of each cell when multiple cells, such as in a 6S Lipo battery, are connected. The battery connector used is an XT60 connector.

docs.title: Setting Up Charger
docs.text:
Open the box and find the cables. The first cable is a banana plug to XT60 plug converter. Connect the two banana cables to the charger, paying attention to the red (+) and black (-) colors.

Next, connect the balance port extension board. Connect the balance board extension cable from the box to the charger main unit, and then connect the cable to the extension board.

Plug the charger's main power cable into a wall outlet and turn on the power switch on the back of the main unit.

docs.title: Charger Setting
docs.text:
The charger consists of two independently operating units in one main body; Unit 1 controls the left port, and Unit 2 controls the right port.

When you first start the charger, the PROGRAM SELECT screen will appear. Use the (+) and (-) buttons to select the Lithium BATT screen, then press the ▶️ button to select it. The LiPo Balance CHG screen will then appear.

Next, connect the battery. After connecting the battery, check that the voltage setting is at 22.2V (6S). If the voltage setting is incorrectly set to 18.5 (5S) or similar, press the ▶️ button to make it blink, then set it to 22.2V (6S).

Next, press and hold the ▶️ button to start charging. The charger will check if the connected battery's voltage matches the charging specs, and if not, an error will appear.

If everything is normal, press the ▶️ button once more to start charging. Wait about 2 hours for a full charge.

While charging, you can press the (+) button to check the voltage of each cell. If the voltage of a particular cell is too low or too high, it is likely that there is a problem with the battery, so it is recommended to stop charging the battery.

By pressing the (–) button, you can view the charging parameters. Here, you can check whether the final voltage is set appropriately, as well as how the charge capacity cut-off and charge time cut-off are configured. If you wish to change these settings, please refer to the manufacturer's user manual.

docs.title: Battery Storage Mode
docs.text:
Lithium polymer batteries used in drones should not be stored for more than a week in a fully discharged or fully charged state, as this can shorten battery lifespan and cause malfunctions. Therefore, when storing drone batteries for an extended period without use, it is recommended to charge or discharge each cell to the storage voltage of 3.8V.

On the charger, press the ▶️ button to make the charger mode setting blink, then press the (-) or (+) button to switch from Balance CHG to Storage mode. Next, press and hold the ▶️ button to enter Storage mode.

docs.title: Why Are Drone Flight Logs Needed?
docs.text: Images collected from the drone contain the camera's GPS information in the EXIF data. However, to use more accurate GPS information and altitude data, you can use the drone's Flight log. Drone altitude information is measured using a down-facing LiDAR, which is useful for image alignment and predicting GSD. The GEMINI-App utilizes drone logs to synchronize the timestamp of images captured by the drone with the GPS timestamps in the log, replacing the image's original GPS information with the drone's GPS coordinates and altitude data.

docs.title: How to Download Drone Flight Log
docs.text:
After the flight, you can connect Mission Planner to download the log.

  1. Connect the drone to the computer using a USB cable.

  1. Launch the Mission Planner app.

  1. Press the CONNECT button to connect to the drone.

  1. Select the "DataFlash Logs" tab and press the "Download DataFlash Log Via Mavlink" button.

  1. When the Log Downloader window appears, (1) check the logs to download and (2) select Download Selected Logs to download. Check the right-side "Output:" to confirm that the log download is complete.

  1. The downloaded log can be found at C:\Users\PAIBL\Documents\Mission Planner\logs\QUADROTOR\1.

  1. Upload the downloaded log using the GEMINI-App. Select the logs with the extension *.bin that correspond to the date of the drone images to upload.

docs.title: Introduction to Ground Control Points (GCPs)
docs.text:
• Definition and purpose of GCPs: Ground Control Points (GCPs) are points on the ground with known latitude, longitude, and altitude used to georeference remote sensing images. This involves placing markers on the ground and measuring their positions using GPS or other methods. The size of the GCPs can vary depending on the resolution of the remote-sensing imagery.

  • Importance of GCPs in drone surveying and mapping: GCPs' positional accuracy affects the positional accuracy of remote sensing images. They also provide ground truth key points for drone image processing.

    For more information, refer to;

    Ground control points: why are they important? | Pix4D

    How Do I Use Ground Control Points?

docs.title: Types of Ground Control Points
docs.text:
• Common types of GCPs used in drone remote sensing: Remote sensing often utilizes identifiable fixed objects with known latitude and longitude values obtainable from sources like Google Maps or other satellite images. However, agricultural fields sometimes need dedicated GCPs due to the need for identifiable and stationary objects. In drone remote sensing, GCPs (Ground Control Points) are either installed in the field as portable tarp-like GCPs for each drone flight or they are left in place throughout the remote sensing project. GCPs are typically designed as checkerboard patterns for easy identification in digital images and are placed in the field.

  • Examples of GCPs Example of GCP near Golden Gate Bridge

    Example of a GCP plate in the field

docs.title: Setting Up Ground Control Points
docs.text:
• GCPs for Low Altitude Drone Remote Sensing For low-altitude, high-resolution drone remote sensing, GCPs (Ground Control Points) the size of a Letter or A4 paper are sufficient for identification. For example, when acquiring imagery at an altitude of 10 meters using a DJI Phantom 4, a resolution of 0.27cm/pixel can be achieved. This means a GCP made with Letter-size paper would appear approximately 80x100 pixels.

  • Example GCP file used in GEMINI Project The GCPs are designed with a checkered pattern for easy identification in aerial imagery. To prevent confusion when numbers are flipped (e.g., 6 and 9), an underline has been added to each number. PDF files for GCPs numbered 1 through 16 are attached, along with Microsoft PowerPoint format files. Download GCP PDF | Download GCP PowerPoint

docs.title: GCP location selection criteria
docs.text:
• Total Number of GCPs For a typical drone remote sensing project, it is advisable to have 5 to 10 GCPs (Ground Control Points) evenly distributed across the field to be surveyed.

  • Choosing optimal locations (e.g., corners of buildings) When utilizing existing terrain features as GCPs, it is recommended to select points where the color of the terrain changes or corners as GCPs.

  • Avoiding obstructions and shadows If there are objects taller than the GCPs in the vicinity, shadows may be cast on the GCPs or they may be obscured in images depending on the relative positions of the drone and the GCPs. Therefore, such locations should be avoided, or obstacles should be removed.

docs.title: Build Instructions

Setup:

  • Bore a hole in the side of the enclosure to size for a cable gland. Drill the hole as low as possible on the side to allow the Arduino USB cable to be inserted with a minimal bend. Insert a cable gland into the hole.
  • Secure the Arduino and the bluetooth module in the bottom of the enclosure. Secure the thermocouple module (with wire connected) to the inside side of the box opposite the hinge with its pins facing away from the cable gland.
  • Attach the temperature / humidity sensor to the top of the enclosure if using a radiation shield. If not, attach the sensor on the side of the enclosure.
  • See bottom of page for the internals of a completed weather station and clarification on placement of components.

Arduino Wiring Guide:

docs.title: Soldering Guide
docs.text:
• Use the example soldered datalogger board (shown below) for reference throughout the soldering process.
  • On three distinct, well-spaced rows of the prototyping area of the datalogger, solder 5-pin, 6-pin, and 3-pin male JST-XH headers. Leave the bottom two rows of the prototyping area untouched. The image below uses rows R1, R5, and R9, leaving R11 free for later. See underside soldering here.
  • Solder a wire from the 5V source to R11 for easier access to the source later on. Solder a wire from the board GND to another point on R11. For convenience, the 5V and GND can also be soldered to the 3-pin header at this time (as shown).

  • NOTE: All pins referred to for soldering on the board reference the digital pins on the right side, not the analog inputs on the left.

  • 5-pin header: Connect the first (leftmost) pin to P13. Connect the next pin to P4. Connect the third pin to P12. Connect the fourth pin to the 5V source. Connect the final pin to GND. See soldered board after this step here.

  • 6-pin header: The outer pin on either side will be unused. Connect the second pin (leftmost pin in use) to P6. Connect the third pin to P5. Connect the fourth pin to GND. Connect the fifth pin (rightmost pin in use) to the 3.3V source. See soldered board after this step here.
  • 3-pin header: Connect the first (leftmost) pin to the 5V source and the last (rightmost) pin to GND if these were not already connected. Connect the second pin to P2.

docs.title: Example Soldered Board
docs.text: • The final soldered board should look similar to this:

docs.title: Assembly
docs.text:
• With three distinctly colored wires (sized appropriately to reach the temperature / humidity sensor from the board), use female JST-XH crimp terminals and a crimp tool to crimp the ends of each wire. Connect the ends of each wire to 3-pin female JST-XH Headers. Repeat this process for five wires to length for the thermocouple module.
  • When connecting the crimped wires to the female headers, pay close attention to how the header will connect with the previously soldered male headers.
  • Using four distinctly colored wires (sized to reach the bluetooth module), connect the ends of each wire to the middle four pins of 6-pin female JST-XH headers.
  • Connect the female wire headers to the properly sized male headers on the board. The 6-pin connector should be connected to the bluetooth module, with the 5-pin and 3-pin connectors going to the thermocouple module and through the cable gland to the temperature / humidity sensor respectively. See wires correctly connected to the female headers and board here.
  • To ensure that the wires are connected properly, one can match the pin connected to the voltage source with the VCC or GND pin on the respective component. Pay attention to which wire is connected to each pin.
  • Connect the Arduino USB cable through the enclosure. If the cable gland included in the linked enclosure is used, some material will have to be shaved from the corners of the USB-B end of the cable.
  • Attach the thermocouple wire to the module's input. Depending on the style of thermocouple used, it may be necessary to solder the thermocouple to the module.
  • Attach the datalogger (with a CR1220 battery and SD Card in place) to the Arduino.
  • If using a radiation shield, attach the radiation shield to the top of the box, covering the temperature / humidity sensor.
